utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Harhoff being absent, today we sit pursuant to the provisions of Rule 15 bis. Ms. Marcus, you are to continue and to be concluding soon, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we had to finish because that was the close of working hours. The doctor had been examined and to give his interpretation of certain documents, and my view is that the doctor cannot act as an expert witness here and provide explanation as to how this could or could not be assessed. This is something to be done by an expert witness, as I see it. Therefore, the doctor cannot interpret documents and everything else that is to be addressed by an expert witness. I remember that we began a discussion about paramedial right and paramedial left, things like that, and I think this is something an expert witness should do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is your response to that, Ms. Marcus?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness can be of assistance to the Court in providing information based on his professional expertise. He can assist the Chamber in deciding on the narrow issue which arose in relation to sniping incident number 5. The exhibit in question was originally put to the Court by the Defence and we are seeking merely to ask the doctor to assist the court in explaining this document. I would also like to point out that during the cross-examination of a previous witness, a major general, the Defence put to that witness numerous questions based on his professional training, his professional knowledge of weaponry, rules of engagement, et cetera, and that witness, without being certified as an expert witness, answered questions based on his professional expertise in those areas. He was also asked to assess certain situations in which he did not directly conduct an investigation but he was in a -- he was -- due to his position and due to the fact that those investigations were conducted by his subordinates, he provided his professional opinion. Dr. Nakas is no different, I would submit. As with the doctor who testified earlier in this case, these hospital records are a mechanism to officially tender material that would otherwise require the Prosecution to call scores of medical professionals to speak to each record individually. This is -- Dr. Nakas is a highly trained physician. His authority during the relevant time included not only supervising all medical procedures in operation of the state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think that's the point. I don't think there's any question about his proficiency. The point, really, is that if he's giving evidence that is expert evidence under the rules, there is a particular procedure to be followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And there are certain procedural requirements, and had you followed those requirements, you would have produced a report by the doctor, given notice to the Defence so that they would have had time to assess it and to determine their response to it. I quite agree that he's able to give the evidence, but it is evidence of an expert nature. Exceptionally I'm going to allow it, but if the Defence requires time to determine their response to it, I believe I'll be obliged to allow them the time. The doctor is here as a fact witness. You didn't call him as an expert witness. And that's the point which is being made by the Defence, and there is merit in it. And in future you should follow the rules so that the Defence can have the opportunity of determining their response to what is, in fact, expert evidence. Let me ask Mr. Tapuskovic. Mr. Tapuskovic, I find that there is merit in your submission, but you may very well be in a position to cross-examine the doctor on the basis of the preparation that you have made. And this is my inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, over the weekend we discussed this problem that has arisen and we have taken certain positions regarding this issue that has already been raised by the Prosecution. But this is a matter of principle. The doctor put his signature in order to verify the documents that had been prepared by other physicians. We did not object to that. We merely think that, apart from this case and the continuation of the examination, if it happens that this will be the only case, and we could allow the Prosecution to finish their examination about this particular incident, but if this happens with dozens of other reports that the doctor has only verified and that he would be examined by the Prosecution about those, then I truly believe that this Chamber should take a position to allow at least this but to restrict this to only this one document. His expert opinion should not be sought about other documents. We are not denying that he has enough professional expertise to answer these kinds of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Tapuskovic. I understand what you have said. In future, when you bring witnesses who are going to give expert evidence, then you must follow the provisions of Rule 94 bis and prepare a report, notify the other party, and time may be saved because the other party may not wish to cross-examine the witness. In this case, I am going to allow it because I have formed the view that there is no prejudice to the Defence. The Defence is in a position to cross-examine. It's for the Chamber to assess the weight of the evidence given. We have to take into consideration all the facts, including those mentioned by Mr. Tapuskovic, as to the weight to be attached to the evidence of the doctor in these matters. So proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Nakas.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: May I please request the court officer kindly to pull up Exhibit D19, 65 ter number 1484, page 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are waiting for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Doctor, on Thursday, during our last session, we were looking at the surgical report for Dzenana Sokolovic. You had just informed the Court that the liver is on the right side, and you were in the process of describing for the Court a blast injury. I'd like to continue from there, please, sir. Doctor, could you please explain for the Court what would cause a blast injury.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the velocity and the power of the projectile, when it passes through the air and through certain tissues, they create certain stream, and this augments the impact. This is the transferred power of the projectile, which is being then transmitted through the tissue and causes the impact on the surrounding tissue in this particular area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am truly sorry that I have to react again. This is not only medical science. We now have introduced another science, and it's being sort of leading, and this is a completely new science. This is not only medicine. Perhaps we should need to hear the opinion of some other experts. I think this is something up to you, Your Honours, to assess and judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic. Ms. Marcus, what I'm going to require you to do is to lay a foundation for this witness to give this kind of evidence. As far as I'm aware, you have not laid any foundation which would suggest that this witness has this kind of expertise. He is a doctor, but for several years he's been working in an administrative capacity. What was the measure of his medical expertise that would allow him to give this kind of evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Understood. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And if you don't succeed in laying this foundation, I will not allow the witness to give this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, are you familiar with medical documents such as the one that you see before you?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw these documents during the preparations as well as all the other documents offered for verification. This one is of a poorer quality than the one that I had seen during the proofing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, on what would you base your familiarity with this kind of a medical report?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each medical history contains certain elements containing interviews, objective findings by the physician regarding the patients; and also, if we are dealing with patients who had undergone surgery, the main surgeon is bound to compile a so-called surgery sheet describing the course of the operation. Therefore, these kinds of documents were available to me in my work with my surgeons when we were doing certain analysis, all the effects of specific surgeries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not his familiarity with the document that is at issue; it is his familiarity with the science that is the foundation for the conclusion set out in the medical document. That's what I need to be assured of.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What experience did he have in these areas, the questions of the impact of bullets, exit and entry wounds. What experience does he have in those matters?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, you have -- you have explained your familiarity with these documents. As a medical doctor, in your capacity in the hospital, what would you -- would you have been in a position to use this information; and if so, in what way would you have used it?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this kind of information was used for the purpose of assessing the appropriateness of certain surgeries that were conducted or performed on patients.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And what would have been your role with regard to assessing these kinds of documents and this kind of information?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not so crucial as the role of the surgeon and the team who were directly involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: On what do you base your knowledge that you've provided of the surgical report and the contents therein?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does he have any practical experience in these matters? Did he actually carry out any operations of this nature?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Doctor, could you comment for the Court, please, on any practical experience you have particularly with these kinds of injuries?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I am not a surgeon. I am a specialist in infectious diseases, not a surgeon who would perform operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think he's capable of giving this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: May I ask one follow-up question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Just one last one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Doctor, would it have required surgical training for a physician to be able to understand a blast injury and explain it?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my studies I passed an exam in general surgery and war surgery and therefore I used this knowledge that I acquired in that period. I also had an exam in forensics which also provides you with a certain amount of knowledge in this area. But this is not my specific area of expertise, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: My ruling on this particular point is that this witness does not have the required expertise to give this kind of evidence. It is true that he would have been exposed by his studies to matters of this kind. He indicated that in his studies he covered forensic science and blast injuries. But he has no specialised knowledge in this area to give this kind of expert evidence, and it is expert evidence. The Prosecution must call a witness with the required expertise to give this kind of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honours. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Doctor, what kind of information did the hospital gather from patients throughout the indictment period with regard to each patient?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each patient that had been referred to the hospital or came on their own seeking medical assistance, in their contacts with the medical staff, had an opportunity to provide information about their illness, how they contracted it, when they contracted it and how; and if we had to deal with injuries, they would provide information of how the injuries had been sustained.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you record whether the patient was a civilian or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this period, for the reasons of monitoring the morbidity, we carried out certain statistical examination of patients and provided statistical data. We divided the patients into two categories, the civilians and members of the armed forces. However, in the records themselves, we took due care when we dealt with members of the armed forces to specify whether their condition was caused within the military service or outside their military service.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you just clarify that a little further? In other words, what would be the difference in how you would record the information if the soldier had been injured within active military service or outside of that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases these records were kept by the medical corps in order for them to monitor the medical condition of the members of the armed forces. Our records, however, dealt very little with that aspect. When they dealt with the patients in the emergency unit, we just specified or recorded that the patient had been injured, and we recorded his or her health condition.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What was it in the rules of the hospital or the medical community that required you to note down whether the patient was a civilian or affiliated with the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was simply a sort of agreement that we had in the city of Sarajevo to monitor the number of casualties and injuries sustained by both the civilian population and the military population.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: If a family member, the wife or the child, of a soldier were to come in as a patient, would they be listed down as a soldier or as a civilian in the hospital records?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases they were recorded as civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: When you interviewed patients coming into the hospital, did you learn about the incident in which they were injured?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases the patient who came to the emergency ward, and when they provided information about their condition, they also provided information about how they had contracted the disease or sustained the injury. These were the basic data provided for the medical term and enable them to establish the diagnosis and decide which procedure to apply in each particular case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Doctor, did you generally learn from patients or persons who came with them to the hospital what the origin of fire was of their injury?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often the patients provided this information and they thought it more important to tell us where and how it happened to them rather than how they actually felt and what the wounds they had sustained. They were more involved in providing information about how the injury was incurred and where it had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you compare your ability to gather this information from patients as it was before the war as compared with how it was in -- between August 1994 and November 1995?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most certainly in peacetime the number of patients who used to come to the hospital was almost negligible in terms of injuries, and those injuries were nothing like those that had happened during the war years of 1994 and 1995. The second difference was in the extent of burden on medical teams who were understaffed and didn't have enough time to devote the best attention to each patient by entering their details on records. They were more focused on identifying the condition and treating their injuries and other problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you gather statistical information based on the records?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that since 1992 and in 1994 and 1995 as well, we relied mostly on the humanitarian aid, including medicines, medical supplies, and fuel. The basic elements that we used to calculate the quantities of medicine, bandages, sutures and other supplies were those acquired on the number of people that had been treated in a certain period of time. Therefore, we kept daily records, weekly records, and monthly records.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And did these statistics include the type of injury sustained?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In certain cases this statistical data, if we were required to provide them, had those characteristics as well. For a certain period of time we were required to provide information about the number of amputations carried out on patients in order to know the number of people for whom certain material had to be prepared, for prosthetic procedures and for alleviating their conditions. The same applies to the injuries sustained by shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did your statistical numbers include numbers of civilians as compared with number of soldiers treated in your facility?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of our statistics distinguished between civilians and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And if a soldier had been injured on a weekend, when not on active duty, not in uniform, unarmed, would that soldier be listed as a civilian or as a soldier in your hospital records?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What percentage would you say, approximately, of the soldiers you treated were wounded when off duty?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although we didn't keep any precise records, I would say that about a third of the soldiers had sustained injuries off duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Court the kinds of injuries suffered by the civilians whom you treated in the period between August 1994 and November 1995?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part the injuries were a result of shelling or shrapnel. Sometimes they were caused by bullets or by sniping. As far as the files that I've looked at, I can say a lot of the patients would come in with mental disturbances caused by the shelling, firing, and everything else that went on in Sarajevo back in 1994 and 1995. The number of those who came calling with some form of mental disturbance was very often greater than those who came in with various wounds and injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, you provided for the Prosecution a statistical chart of sniping victims treated in your hospital between August 1994 and November 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: May I request the court officer to put up on the monitor this chart: It is 65 ter number 2877, page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, can you please describe for the Court what this document is that we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two documents. The one on the right, on my right -- well, it's just one document now. These are two tables, spreadsheets, containing information about people who suffered sniping injuries and who were admitted to the Sarajevo General Hospital. One is in relation to August 1994 and the other, the general number of people who suffered sniping injuries in January and December 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Who prepared this document?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Doctor, could you please --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now my microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm sorry, could you please repeat the answer to the question of who prepared this document.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I prepared this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Where did you prepare the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I prepared this in my office in the General Hospital just before I came to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What documents did you use to prepare this report?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To prepare this report, I went through all the protocols of the emergency unit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to ask you, Doctor, to please repeat the answer to that question - the microphone went off in between - explaining what documents you used to prepare this report.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To prepare this report, I used protocols of the emergency centre that were kept between August 1994 and October 1995. There were six or seven of those with records on all patients admitted to the emergency centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Doctor, can you confirm that this report is a true and accurate reflection of those monthly reports?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This, in essence, is a true reflection of the daily examinations conducted on patients who were admitted and recorded in the protocols each day between August 1994 and October 1995. These were called on a daily basis and arrive in the emergency centre, the patients.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Are these the complete number of victims of sniper injuries treated in a State Hospital between those dates of August 1994 through October 1995?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a list of all the wounded of Sarajevo who claimed they had been wounded by sniping. The doctors would establish that, and then this particular piece of information would be added to a patient's file.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Just for clarification, Doctor, this chart does not include any sniping victims treated in any other of the medical facilities in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct. The number includes those who were treated in the General Hospital or the State Hospital of Sarajevo alone. It is possible that a rather small number of these patients had been sent over from the emergency unit where they had first been seen to and then sent on to our hospital. So this number does not include those who were treated in health clinics or the University Medical Centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In total, between August 1994 and October 1995, how many civilians, adults and children together, did you treat for wounds due to sniping?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The total overall this time would be 115 cases; 74 of these were civilian casualties, eight of which were children.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this chart into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P108, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Doctor, can you estimate approximately what percentage of the total number of patients you treated during the time period between August 1994 and November 1995 were civilian victims of sniping and shelling, please?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the total of those treated throughout that time, about 10 per cent of them were sniping casualties and about 90 per cent were shelling casualties.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did the number of civilian casualties of sniping and shelling fluctuate in this period?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. There were certain months and days when the number was smaller and months and days when the number was considerably larger.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: To what do you attribute this fluctuation?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fluctuation was normally influenced by increased movement of citizens across Sarajevo or by increased shelling and such injuries as were normally caused by a new round of shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You have seen the schedule of incidents to the indictment which the Prosecution seeks to prove as examples of the sniping and shelling campaign; is that correct, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of these incidents based on your work in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had already got used to greater numbers of injured civilians being admitted throughout 1993 and 1994. So the 1994 and 1995 period wouldn't be marked any particular way; only the figure was beyond something we had expected. What I remember most of all was the Markale shelling on the 28th of August 1995, and that's when the hospital really stepped in.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you remember about that incident, please.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the circumstances that preceded this incident. It was a rather peaceful day when suddenly one could hear the sound of sirens, mostly car sirens and not ambulances. I had a conference with some colleagues and people were saying things like, Maybe someone is getting married. However, the original concerns were confirmed when the first injured persons started streaming into the hospital. I still remember the moment clearly, because I stopped the meeting, and along with a small number of other people who were at the emergency centre at the time - a small number because we had not expected to have more injured persons coming in than usual - we admitted the first wounded. We carried out some sort of a triage and we called on some people who were outside the hospital at the time to come in and give us a hand, since at this point we were beginning to expect more casualties coming in on that particular day than was usual.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you recall, Doctor, if the injured were civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I do remember is that most of those people were wearing civilian clothes. Given the location of the incident, one thing is certain: There was no fighting going on there. And if any soldiers just happened to be there, they were there for the market, to buy their groceries, and not for any other reason; meaning nearly 100 per cent of the casualties that we treated on that day were civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Are there any other incidents on the list that you remember personally from your own experience, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another similar incident in June 1995, the time the radio-television centre was hit by an air bomb. A number of those injured during that particular incident received medical assistance in our hospital. I met a number of those people later on. I talked to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was this incident different in any way from other shelling incidents?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in a way. In addition to the fact that there were injuries caused by shrapnel or bits of the building falling off, there were also those who had suffered the so-called blast syndrome. Everyone knows what that looks like and one doesn't need to be an expert in any medical field to recognise and identify the effect of a blast shock on a patient.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you describe, in your opinion, what the blast shock looks like.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I pointed out already, when there is a powerful explosion, there is air turbulence, so this impact caused by the turbulence is much greater when an air bomb goes off. Those in the vicinity of the explosion suffer injuries to internal organs in which there is air - the lungs, the stomach, the middle ear. There is increased air pressure and there can be ruptures caused to certain tissues in those cavities. One thing that must be noted is that very often this is not easy to spot externally. It is not necessarily accompanied by shrapnel wounds bleeding or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Doctor, you have much experience treating both wounded soldiers as well as wounded civilians. Based on this experience, what would you say was the impact of the shelling and the sniping in Sarajevo between August 1994 and November 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you mean by the impact of the shelling and the sniping? That's at a fairly general level.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What kind of impact are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I was referring to his observation, based on the patients who came in, the impact on the civilian population who were treated in his facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let's hear from the doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Generally speaking, in addition to the immediate impact, meaning the injuries caused by firearms, there were other kinds of impact on the mental state of patients, whether they were injured or not. There was a possibility every day that you might be killed or wounded, and this certainly had mental ramifications, psychological ramifications, and this applied to children and adults in equal measure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Doctor, do you have any personal lasting effects of the war on yourself that you can tell the Court about?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my capacity as hospital administrator, I have knowledge of certain experiences of what occurred over the past years. Had it not been for all of that, Abdulah Nakas and Dr. Sehovic, one of our two famous war surgeons, would still be alive; they would not have died at age 60 or thereabouts. Another very able anesthesiologist would not have died aged under 65 or thereabouts. What affected me personally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question that you were asked was whether you had any personal lasting effects of the war, effect on yourself. Could you address that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may not even be aware of the consequences that I have suffered yet. However, I read this book by Professor Richard Mollica who is the head of the war trauma institute at the Harvard Institute in Boston. It's called, "Healing Invisible Wounds," and my war story is right there, my own trauma. He, as a psychiatrist, believes that I must have suffered some sort of a war trauma, although I may not have been aware of it. It may have been my reaction to that trauma that preserved me from its potentially negative effect. I used whatever energy I had at the time, whatever energy I would muster up, to help other people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Marcus. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I could have the lectern, please. Thank you. Your Honours, I will not be wasting any time with this. There is this letter that I'll be tendering later on. I would like to use this opportunity to tell you, I mentioned that I'll be seeking your intervention for the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina to meet certain conditions. I can tell you that -- well, it's in progress. I'll probably be getting the documents on the 2nd of February. My investigators will take delivery. On the 5th of February, my investigators will be able to go through the archives of the Supreme Command of the BH army. So for the time being, I'll not be submitting that motion or, indeed, burdening the Chamber with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nakas, I am Defence counsel for Mr. Dragomir Milosevic, Branislav Tapuskovic, attorney-at-law from Belgrade. You have provided a number of statements, quite a number, and they were all tendered under Rule 65 ter. I will be using no more than three of those, although there must be a total of seven or eight. The one dated the 10th to 12th of November, 1995, which is the first statement that you gave in November 1995. The next thing is a statement taken by the Prosecution in September, and finally, the one dated the 16th of January, 1997. Before I start with these, I, of course, will not be asking for any explanations regarding what the Prosecutor wanted to know about -- but if you could please briefly explain what the median axis is. It's something that goes down the central axis of the human body. It's an axis that divides the human body into equal halves. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that casualties would come in. They always knew where they had been hit from and they would tell you; is that right? Not you personally, the doctors there. Yes, please, if you could comment.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first impressions upon arriving at the emergency centre would be about being hit --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where they were hit from?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there would normally be assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Given the state they were in, they were still able to say that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in as far as they were aware of it, them or the people accompanying them to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. A while ago you spoke about the so-called blast syndrome, which is something that I'm aware of as far as bombs are concerned. But you started talking about the blast syndrome also in relation to -- the Prosecutor asked you in relation to sniping. Can there be any such thing as a blast syndrome when talking about sniping? Because there's no air impact.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been a misinterpretation. It was not about the blast syndrome --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me hear Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: It appears to me that learned counsel is attempting to ask the same kinds of questions of the Doctor that he objected to the Prosecution putting, based on his expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When you carried on your examination-in-chief, I did allow him to give fairly general evidence about the blast but not anything which would require specialised knowledge. And I believe this question is at that level. Mr. Tapuskovic, you must remember that I did not allow the witness to give evidence which, in my view, required specialised knowledge in relation to the blast syndrome, and that resulted from the submission that you made which I upheld. I'll allow you to ask this question and any other question which is at a very general level, which does not require specialised knowledge. This kind of question, I think, falls into that category, so let us hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. If my learned colleague, the Prosecutor, had asked the question as she had done just now, I wouldn't have objected. However, I do appreciate your intervention and I may withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will start with what my learned colleague finished off. Mr. Nakas, your statement given between the 10th and 12th of November, 1995, and the table that is contained therein --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like this document, 65 ter number 02839 be placed in front of the witness, and we will first go to page 5, paragraph 1 of the English version, and page 4, paragraph 2 from the bottom in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are waiting for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English version, for Mr. Nakas, could we please have page 4, second paragraph from the bottom, and for Their Honours, page 5, paragraph 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It begins with "The year of 1994 ..." Can you see that? Paragraph 2 from the bottom, Mr. Nakas, can you see it?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true what it reads here: "The year of 1994 was better than the others," and then you go on to say: "In the first half of the year, the number of patients was only 431 as compared with 1996." First of all, is this correct? Can you tell me?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Compared to the previous years, 1992 and 1993, in absolute terms and according to the statistics, there were fewer injured people in 1994 than in the previous years. It is obvious that in 1992 there were 2.400 and in the next year there were 3.411, and in 1994 it was a considerably lower number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the next passage, please. Maybe it's not necessary for me to read it out to you. Just look at what it says in the last sentence, which says: "Only those who were wounded or who had an acute problem which affected their life would be admitted. All others we did not admit." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since the beginning of the war until the beginning of this month, so you are talking about this in November 1995, when the war was still going on, you said that you had treated 8.000 patients, and until the end of October it can be broken down as follows, and then you list the table. Is everything that I read correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What I just read to you.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The next question: Neither here nor anywhere else you spoke nothing about the number of the people wounded, but you never mentioned sniping. How is it possible that all those people in 1994 had been wounded by sniping?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My statement refers primarily to the years of 1992 and 1993 because that was the subject of investigation. These were just the comments about the general state of affairs without going into details as to what kind of injuries were sustained. And in that context, maybe the number is not as relevant as the nature of what had been going on. In other words, in the interview I was not asked to separate the number of casualties caused by sniping or shelling, and in this particular case this was asked of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly - I would like to be mistaken - you said that the Prosecutor asked you about the people who suffered injuries in 1994 and 1995, between August 1994 and November 1995, when you made this statement, and you said that they were all victims of sniping. Is that what you said just now?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that they were all sniper victims. It was just a table extracting the number of people who were sniper victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So all these 607 in 1994 and 668 in 1995 were sniper victims?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't get it right. The total number that you just mentioned, there were 115 of them and they were included in the table made in January. Absolutely in my first statement there was no question asked of me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I understand, but I am entitled to comment on this. If you said that by mid-1994 there were 431 casualties in 1994 - I'm not good at figures - you say here that there was a total of 670 in 1994. If, as you said, there were 431 victims in the first half of the year, if we deduce this number from the figure stated here, it seems that between -- from August onwards, there were 176 victims. Now I'm talking about the year 1995. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If your arithmetic is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does this figure of 176 include those wounded in Markale?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm only talking about 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go for a moment to 1995.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does this figure of 668 include all the victims at Markale, 80-something?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It only includes the people who came to the hospital. This is not the number of victims in Markale; only the people who came to see me from Markale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if we compare the years 1994 and 1995, the total figures for these years, with the previous period, don't you find that there is an amazing difference in numbers?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in total numbers, but not in the nature of wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, was the number of casualties affected to a great extent by the offensive, an all-out offensive, carried out by the BH army throughout the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly. A number of injured members of armed forces are included in this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Another question in this respect. If this offensive had an impact on this, how is it possible that the number of civilians who were casualties in 1995 was greater than the number of soldiers wounded in that same year? It says here 388 civilians and 280 troops. How is it possible that more civilians were killed in an offensive than soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secondly, this is not the total number, this was just the number that refers to the State Hospital in Sarajevo which accounts for only one-tenth of all the capacities, which means that nine times this number were taken care of in other institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is your report, and if we receive some other report, I am going to deal with this. I would like you to explain to me this huge difference between the number of killed soldiers, wounded soldiers, and wounded civilians.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, this is the number of wounded taken care of in our hospital. What is the number taken care of by other hospitals I cannot really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have -- I think that I sought enough explanation regarding the figures. And then you go on to say: "It should be noted that the military totals include people who are soldiers but were injured as civilians, for example, while shopping, et cetera." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You want to say that while these things were happening in the city of Sarajevo, the soldiers walked around in civilian clothes and unarmed.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning carrying the arms, specifically automatic weapons, could not be seen frequently in Sarajevo. The only weapon that the armed forces carried were small arms, and nobody took an automatic gun to a market.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And they could walk around without any arms?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to avoid using a map because it takes up a lot of time, but if I can please be helped in having map number D222.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could I have the document ID number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is up to my associates to provide this. D22 has been tendered as a Defence Exhibit. It's DD000261. My apologies to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: This one?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has it. Why don't you have it? With apologies to Milton, they also [Realtime transcript read in error "only"] serve those who sit and wait. Have you found the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have shown us last time, Dr. Nakas, where your hospital is.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you also mentioned the hospital at Kosevo.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned First State Clinic. Can you show me, please, where the Jezero Hospital is?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please mark it.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just to ensure that you have what I said correctly, it is "they also serve" not "they only serve."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Have you shown it?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark it with the letter J?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If we are talking about the confrontation or demarcation line between the warring parties, this hospital is very close to it.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time was that a hospital or did it have some other purpose?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What time? You mean in 1994? In 1994 it was an abandoned hospital, in 1992, after the first shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any military or police units in this hospital?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about the Bethania Hospital? Was that a maternity ward?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was another facility, the construction of which started back in 1976 and it is far away from the Jezero Hospital, towards Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please show it.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was it within the area of responsibility of BH army?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the area of demarcation line and they are not quite acquainted with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: BH army?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was under the control of our forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any police or military troops there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. It was a facility under construction, and it just had concrete walls and foundations, and it's still in the same state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark it with B.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure where it is exactly located.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right, Doctor, it's not of such importance. The hospital on Skerliceva Street, I think that was a children's hospital in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only an out-patient children's clinic on Skerliceva Street that was never a hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please show it.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is approximately here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just approximately. It's not crucially important. Perhaps where you have this little cross.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have Mejtas, you have a big park here. This is the Skerliceva Street, and that was an out-patient clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did it do during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was still a children's hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was it ever targeted?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was targeted a few times but it was not directly in the line of fire because it's surrounded by buildings.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It's impossible to translate this overlapping conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic and Doctor, the interpreters are finding it difficult to follow you. You speak the same language, so observe a pause between question and answer, in the interests of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see that it's displayed, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's right here, the letter D.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that this is in the center of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There was another hospital, the hospital for lung diseases. I think it was called Potrastovina [phoen].

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Whereabouts was it, exactly?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's right next to the confrontation line between the army of Republika Srpska and the BH army. No, it's a lot further from -- then my own hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was there during the war?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Patients and doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if people were at risk in that hospital?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as much as anyone else in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, that's what you mean. Fine, thank you. Are you aware of the two hospitals that were on the Republika Srpska army side, "Ernest Grin"?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It was emptied --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Abandoned. There was no one there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No one there for safety reasons, for the sake of the patients' safety. And the same applies to the mental hospital near Jagomir, that had been emptied, too?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, back in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The hospital of which you were later director -- before that, you used to be a JNA hospital; right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a JNA hospital, the third in terms of importance throughout the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At your time there, after the JNA had withdrawn, in that same hospital compound there was a clinic used by the garrison, a clinic used to treat military personnel exclusively. Was this clinic used for military purposes during the war, or was there a military unit that was stationed there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was the rehabilitation centre. I mentioned that when asked if there were any military facilities within the State Hospital perimeter. I pointed out that there was a building that was mobilised for the rehabilitation of soldiers, members of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There was probably some military security around the building.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just some police guarding the perimeter, the Marin Dvor police station reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: They were armed?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the policemen were not carrying any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please say, what about within the perimeter of the Kosevo Hospital? Was the 105th Mountain Brigade not there, with its forward command post right there at the Kosevo hospital, in an unfinished building? I found that in an order of the commander of the 12th Division, which I will be tendering. Do you remember the command post of that brigade being there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you say in relation to your own hospital, at a mere 200 metres from you, in peacetime there used to be the Zagreb Hotel.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The Zagreb Hotel during the fighting was full of policemen going about certain duties that they had, which very often involved the BH army; right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe. This is something you know. I know it was an abandoned facility. I don't know who was there, reservists, policemen, it's certainly possible. But this was certainly not a military target, if that's what you're implying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There were special units stationed there.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not something that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this is our usual time for our first morning break. Do you think I should press on or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we'll take the break now and we'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, as much as I don't like being a timekeeper, I must inform you that the examination-in-chief was roughly two hours. You have utilised roughly half an hour. You will have another hour and a half. You do not have to use that time, of course. You're not obliged to use it. Your questions must be relevant and to the point. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see the accused is not present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed. The accused is now here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I realise that there are some problems with the map. I'm not planning on dwelling on the map, so if it could please be assigned a number the way it is now, and then I will be requesting another map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let that be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can have I the UNPROFOR map, please; 65 ter number 02829, if that could be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I understand correctly, they seek to tender map document ID DD000261 as well as the map as it was marked by the witness. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you confirm that, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honours, the map as marked by the witness will become Exhibit D27 and the map itself will become Exhibit D28.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I perhaps use this opportunity to tender that letter as well, the one that I forgot about when we were examining Mr. Nicolai. It's the letter that I had no English translation of at the time, DD000286 and DD000261. I've just made another mistake, Your Honours. I'll be tendering that a little later because I just made another mistake when I wrote down the numbers. I would like to forge ahead with my questions, since I see the map. It's right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No need for you to mark anything, Doctor, but one thing I would like to, at a distance of 200 metres from the hospital of which you were general manager, was there not the old hospital building, the building of the so-called old hospital?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was perhaps several dozens of metres, not 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, at a distance of 20 metres from you. During the war and between the 10th of August 1994 and November 1995, what was there? Who was there? Who was in that building, soldiers, police?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hospital had been hit in the first months of 1992. It caught fire and burned down. It was virtually a ruin. Throughout 1994 and 1995, and even later on, this was a ruin of a building burned down. No living creatures there except maybe for a handful of stray dogs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about Dragomir Milosevic's time. It wasn't hit during Dragomir Milosevic's time.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had been hit back in 1992. It had all burned down by the time of the events that we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was it not just behind your hospital that there was a -- the two hills, Crni Vrh and Gorica? You know Sarajevo well, don't you? Crni Vrh is 614 metres, and the other hill is 170 metres. Those two were right behind you as well as Debelo Brdo; right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, geographically speaking, Crni Vrh and Gorica. Yes, Debelo Brdo is on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So the mistake is mine. Nevertheless, these positions were being held by the BH army at the time.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Citizens of the city of Sarajevo were there, civilian facilities, houses, residential buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No soldiers at all?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no confrontation line there anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. That was a bit further off. Those hills were within the area of responsibility of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you don't know if there were any military positions there or not, do you?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll only be dwelling on this map briefly. You are and have been for a long time a citizen of Sarajevo. You are familiar with this environment. Debelo Brdo is pretty high up, isn't it? What about Colina Kapa, that was within the BH army zone of responsibility, too, and the peak is at nearly 1.000 metres; right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not 1.000 metres. It's somewhat less.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: About 900; right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think under 900.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is all part of Trebevic isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is one of the hills or ridges belonging to Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about Debelo Brdo? Isn't Debelo Brdo another elevation that was held by the BH army? They had their positions there; right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think the confrontation line ran along Debelo Brdo. It was roughly half, half.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then we have Mojmilo, which is also quite an elevation, quite high and quite long, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mojmilo Brdo, wasn't this a place that throughout the war, or perhaps at the beginning, was held by the BH army which had its position there; right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the second half of 1992 that it was part of the free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have much more on this. Colina Kapa, 940 metres; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Several questions about this. The hills that we discussed, they're down south; right? You had left and then you had right, and then as far as Nedzarici and then over there, you have the hills that we have been discussing. Debelo Brdo, Colina Kapa, Mojmilo. To the north -- I'm not going into any details on this; I'd be wasting a lot of time. To the north there is the hill known as Zuc, 800 metres; right? That's where the BH army positions were; right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And there's Orlic, 876 metres, the peak. The peak was also at the time held by the BH army; right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And we have the neighbourhood of Sokolje, Bresce Brdo, Sabino Brdo. The peak is at 689 metres, and that too at the time was held by the BH army; right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all part of the free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, but it's all to the north; right? If you head right on this map -- left, rather, to the right, these are all hills up above the centre of Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but quite distant from it, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But within the zone of responsibility of the BH army, and posing a threat to all the Serb settlements on the other side; right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably both in geographical and practical terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I won't be dwelling on this anymore. I'd like to return to your statements. I know that I have a time limit. There are seven or eight statements that you made, but I'm using three. The one you gave between the 10th and the 12th of November, 1995, this is 65 ter 02389, paragraph 3. I would like to read the whole paragraph and you can tell me if that is, in fact, the case. I said the English, page 2, paragraph 3; B/C/S, page 2, paragraph 3. I hope you have that in front of you. That's page 2. It's the first page of the actual statement; do you have that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I still have the maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2 of the English, paragraph 3; the same reference for the B/C/S. That's it. That's it. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You see paragraph 3 there, don't you? It reads: "During the aggression ..."

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll read it for your benefit and you confirm, please. "During the aggression on Croatia, some of our staff were deployed to other places in order to be ready to go to the front line. A large number of people went to areas close to the front lines. In 1991 and early 1992 we spent a lot of time working in the hospital near the front line." What you have in mind here is other parts of Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "And we took turns every three weeks. We could in this way see what was going on. We met many people," and then quotation marks, "C". I'm not sure what you mean here, "many people" and then a "C" under quotation marks. Maybe there's something missing. And then it says "Croats."

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's probably a matter of interpretation. Maybe this stands for Croats, people marked with an S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. "We met many people who expressed their political views. It was obvious that we did not believe in the same things. The JNA became more and more involved in politics in Croatia and then in Bosnia." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, sir, you went outside Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was all the same country at that time. Did you ever go to Slovenia? Did you realise what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our units, or rather, members of the former war hospital, were assigned to the Tuzla area and the Banja Luka area for the medical corps there that were supposed to set up war hospitals. They were members of these medical corps, and some of them went to Gradiska, the front line there, and to Banja Luka. And a number of surgeons were working there. I personally was stationed at Tuzla, at Husinska Buna, the intention being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you there. There is no interpretation in French. There is now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: There is now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is now interpretation in French, so you may now continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I would like to hear from you, had you heard that the JNA had been attacked in Slovenia and that the fronts actually were the surrounded barracks in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the information we had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear information that as many as 50 unarmed soldiers had been killed there or even those who had surrendered?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know it wasn't such a high figure. There could have been some accidentally soldiers, but I don't know about over 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say over 50. I am not asking you to say what you don't know. Do you know that also in Croatia there were a large number of surrounded barracks?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was such information in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From the document that I have in front of me - English version of this same document, page 2, the penultimate passage - it begins "On the 6th of April, an aggression started, one person was shot on Vrbanja bridge. We knew what was going to happen. From then until mid-April, many of us who were military left." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before 6th of April, would it be fair to say that in early March a Serbian member of a wedding party was killed at Bascarsija? I may have the location wrong, but at any rate this man was killed there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and he was buried at Bare on the same day when my father, whom I found dead in the street on the 2nd of May, was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after that you say as follows: "After the 2nd of March, when members of the SDS --" do you know who killed your father?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father died of heart attack in front of a tobacconist shop. I found him in a morgue, he was 69 years old in quite good health, and he died of stress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, you said that your father was killed on that same day, or did I not understand you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the killed Serb was buried on the same day at the Bare cemetery where my father was buried as well, whom I found dead in the morgue on the 2nd of March. That was the morgue of the Kosevo Hospital, probably after he had suffered a heart attack in front of the news agent shop close to our house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Above this passage where you talk about the 6th of April, it says as follows: "After March the 2nd, when members of the SDS," which is the Serbian Democratic Party; right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: -- "put up barricades when they realised what could happen." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Right. But isn't it true that they had put up barricades precisely because of this killing and because the SDA, the Party of Democratic Action, had also put up barricades?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: These barricades had nothing to do with the killing of this member of the wedding party. They were the result of the referendum that were positive for the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the course that she decided to take as an independent state. And that was the reaction by the Serbian Democratic Party to the result of the referendum and it had absolutely nothing to do with the killing that took place at Bascarsija.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I presume that you must have read books written by Halilovic, his son, the accused Delic, and many others. Did you read those books?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must disappointment you. I didn't read any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the Official Gazette which says that the status of combatants was granted to all members of the Patriotic League, the Green Berets and other paramilitary units in the spring of 1992? That's what's written in a decision published in the Official Gazette. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that. I know that I was a lieutenant colonel of the JNA and I did not have the status of a combatant granted for the period between 1992 and 1995. I was just an ordinary citizen with a war assignment, and I didn't have the status of a combatant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned your status. You were born in 1949, and I'm a little bit older than you. Do you know -- let us put aside the period between 1945 and 1950, but let's take the period after 1950 until 1990, was it ever the case in the area where we all lived together, was there any more peaceful time and better life in the history of all our peoples there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you ask me, I'm one of those who admit that it was very nice to live during Tito's era.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know that before the 6th of April, that is, in late March, in Sijekovac, around 30 or more Serb civilians were brutally killed in the area held by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you also know that at the same time before the 6th of April, in Glamoc and other areas, a large number of civilians were killed when there was no war operation there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some information about that. What I mentioned is something that I mentioned from my personal experience in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course what you don't know --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you should know this, because this refers to what was happening in Sarajevo. We are going back to this document, last passage on the same page: "I left the hospital on the 8th of April, but my brother, who is also a doctor, was still here, and I was relatively well informed of the events here." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the same day when I left the hospital, that is, on the 8th of April, my brother was mobilised for the Sokolac War Hospital as a surgeon, and with the assistance of his friends he was transferred to Sarajevo, so he came back in mid-April and I had reliable information about what was going on in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you had reliable information, do you know that on or around that date, and I heard that from Dr. Mandilovic who testified here the other day, the hospital had been surrounded for almost a month by members of the Patriotic League and Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't literally surrounded. It was surrounded in order to maintain the spirit of patriotism, not by patriotic forces in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
