utterances.text: Were the barracks in Sarajevo also surrounded?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, they were under the blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any casualties among the JNA soldiers in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, a small number of wounded members of the JNA were treated at the time in the military hospital, which means that it wasn't -- there were not too many casualties, people wounded, if that's what you're referring to. There were probably isolated cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you know what was going on in the hospital -- inside the hospital, there was a special unit in the hospital, as you said in your statement, that had come from Nis, and that was also surrounded during the month of blockade, which was also mentioned by Mr. Mandilovic.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as this special unit was concerned, the day after I left it, the hospital, they were deployed there. I know that my office was given to the commander of this unit. His name was Golub or whatever. But they were not surrounded. They were free to go out with their vehicles, to go to their command headquarters without any restrictions whatsoever. No -- there were no roadblocks and things like that. And these soldiers in the hospital were free to communicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May, is it true that a large number of soldiers were killed on Dobrovoljacka Street?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that incident and I know that a number of members of the then special units deployed in the military hospital headed for Skenderija, and that a number of those soldiers were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Both you and Mr. Mandilovic claim that it was possible to leave the hospital. But after people learned about the incident of the 2nd of May, is it not true that a large number of medical personnel, including Dr. Radulovic, left the hospital and were killed on Dobrovoljacka Street?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was anyone killed?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Radulovic had left the hospital earlier. He wasn't there at all. Colonel -- Dr. Radulovic, as far as I can remember, was the chief of the medical corps and he used to stay at the corps HQ. And he left with a corps command, so none of our doctors had left the hospital and got killed. They were not in the convoy of the staff command that had left these facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So he was killed?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was brought dead on arrival to the hospital, but as to the circumstances of how it happened, I don't know anything about that. The only thing I know is that when I came and became the director of the hospital on the 10th of May, the late Dr. Radulovic was in the morgue of our hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I'd like to object to this historical line of questioning on the grounds of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, explain the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance is that I'm trying to question and challenge certain things established in the Galic judgement, primarily the roots of the conflicts and what was the background. I'm not going to ask the witness about the events in the Galic period. But all of this is something that Dragomir Milosevic is directly being charged with, the incidents in 1992 and the general situation that was conducive to the conflict. Most probably a number of medical staff had left the hospital, which was surrounded, and they never returned because they were killed when the tragedy with the soldiers on Dobrovoljacka Street took place. This is not true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are not to comment on anything. I'm hearing the argument advanced by Mr. Tapuskovic, and I'm about to consider it. You say that this relates to the roots of the conflict and the background, and you say that "all of this is something that Dragomir Milosevic is directly being charged with, the incidents in 1992 and the general situation ... conducive to the conflict." Is it correct to say that he's been charged with these incidents?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the amended indictment, the culpability of Dragomir Milosevic was established by claiming that he was aware of the strategy being employed from the answer that he inherited and took over the same strategy and pursued it. If you pay careful attention to the indictment, it seemed that he developed this strategy back in 1992, and once he took over the command in August 1992, he just continued with it. That is what the indictment says. And I'm trying to prove that Dragomir Milosevic, although he was a JNA officer at the time, had nothing to do with all these things at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where does the indictment say that he developed the strategy back in 1992? Can you direct me to that paragraph of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could do that very easily if you could please just give me three minutes. Not only that. That he took over this strategy from Galic and continued to pursue it. The initial indictment did not contain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You do not have three minutes. You'll have a minute to find it. Let me ask Ms. Marcus if she has anything in reply.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, all I would say in reply is that the indictment begins on the 10th of August, 1994, and does not charge the accused with any events prior to that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That necessarily rules out evidence of incidents before. But would that be your contention?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't say it rules out evidence. But there was quite an extensive line of historical questioning, going back to 1991 in Slovenia, which led us gradually forward. So it was my question, what was the relevance of the extent of the historical line of detailed questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He says it's relevant to the roots of the indictment, of the charges. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, paragraph 13 of the indictment, "when, on the 10th of August --" "when on or about the 10th of August, 1994, Dragomir Milosevic took over control of the corps, he took over -- he inherited this campaign from General Galic. For the next approximately 15 months, he continued to implement this campaign of attacks against the civilian population of Sarajevo." The previous paragraph, it says: "For 44 months, the SRK implemented that campaign." Dragomir Milosevic only stands indicted on the basis of his command responsibility during this time. I could go on, but it's about this first moment where it says that the mens rea was established at this early stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, it's not clear to me how that paragraph substantiates the claim that you're making. What it says is that "Dragomir Milosevic inherited the campaign from General Galic when he took over on the 10th of August, 1994." So it's not clear to me how evidence of what happened before would be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During my case I will try to challenge some of the issues that the judgement seems to have established beyond doubt. I've no time to go into this now, but I'm trying to track down a huge paragraph about this. This was not in the judgement, but then this was quoted as one of the major reasons for his culpability. I can read that for you, Your Honours. "Pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal, Dragomir Milosevic" this is 19, "Dragomir Milosevic is individually criminally responsible for planning and ordering the crimes charged in this indictment. Dragomir Milosevic implemented and authorised the campaign of sniping and shelling of civilians which had the primary purpose of spreading terror within the civilian population of Sarajevo. From May 1992, when he was commander of the SRK's 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade, and from July 1993 when he was the SRK's chief of staff, Dragomir Milosevic knew of the campaign against the civilian population. When he became corps commander from on or about the 10th of August, 1994, Dragomir Milosevic inherited this campaign and proceeded to maintain and further it through direct orders, including orders to launch" and I don't wish to tire you with this, "launch and fire air bombs," so on and so forth. So this is the original indictment -- this is something that wasn't in the original indictment against Dragomir Milosevic, and then this was added and we were left facing a situation where we only had two or three months and we had to start pondering this whole new substance to the indictment that posed an enormous problem for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, our attention has just been drawn to paragraphs which say that from May 1992, when he was commander of the SRK's 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade, and from July 1993, Dragomir Milosevic knew of the campaign against the civilian population. It would appear, then, that there are periods prior to 1994 when the indictment does allege knowledge on the part of Dragomir Milosevic of certain matters relevant to the charges.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The indictment charges the accused under several modes of liability, one of which, of course, is Article 7(3), and the intent behind this paragraph was to show that the knowledge element required to prove that mode of liability was something which began from the first day that the indictment begins, so in other words, from on or about the 10th of August, 1994, that he had knowledge. I'll defer to Your Honours on this, but I would also submit simply that perhaps the doctor is not the right witness to be going into this issues with. But I will certainly defer in terms of relevance to Your Honours' determination, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the Chamber will allow you to pursue that line of questioning, but bear in mind that the doctor may not be able to help you much in relation to this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The doctor is what he is, first and foremost. I'm not asking him to answer military questions; I'm asking him to tell us what he knows. I've been dropping a whole lot of questions along the way precisely for this reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just proceed. You have a tendency to be overly loquacious.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully respect your position, Your Honour, but you had requested an explanation which left us in a helpless position. Two or three months before the beginning of the trial, our strategy had been quite different -- had it not been for this change, it would have been. And now we're facing this huge bulk of new material and all I'm trying to do is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, proceed with the cross-examination. Proceed with the cross-examination. I've already ruled in your favour. Do you not understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My apologies. I will be dropping a lot of questions that I had planned for. But let me go to page 3, paragraph 6 of the English. Same reference in B/C/S. It's the same document, page 3, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You talk about the month of May. You say the 13th through the 16th of May.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that on my screen yet. I do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "The worst period of targeting was 13 to 16 of May, just after they had left. The hospital was hit by about 40 shells of various kinds, mainly tank and artillery shells. The shelling started in the afternoon and that night we emptied all the patient rooms on the south side of the hospital." Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph you say: "It appeared to me that they were intent on destroying vital parts of the hospital. This was a JNA hospital so they knew where everything was. They tried to hit the sterilisation rooms, operating theaters, and also patient rooms on the 5th, 6th ..." and so on and so forth. Right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic spoke about the fact that he wasn't even certain that the hospital had been targeted intentionally, deliberately. But let he ask you something else. There was a special unit in that hospital, special JNA unit, that had arrived from Nis. After this they left the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina altogether and went back to where it had come from. Let me ask you: If they wanted to, they could have blown the whole thing sky high. They were inside, but they never touched any of the vital parts of the building. How do you explain that, if they had wanted to destroy the hospital or any of its vital parts, why didn't they just blow the whole thing sky high when they were there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what we knew, there were no plans for the destruction of the hospital. They wanted to keep it under the control of the Serb forces, because the demarcation line was supposed to run along the Djurejako [phoen] Street and not the bridge. So had the Pofalici battle been a success, the hospital would have remained in territory under the control of the JNA, which means there was absolutely no need or, indeed, intent to destroy the hospital as such. However, on the 9th of May, as soon as the sudden decision was taken to evacuate, there was no time and no chance to do it in such a brief period of time. Therefore, our conclusion, based on whatever information we had, was what followed was deliberate targeting of all those different parts of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about the vital parts of the hospital, the operating theaters? It all worked smoothly; right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which time period are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From August to --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In August, when we left in May, we never went back until late in 1994 and early 1995. And I'm talking about the north wing, the one that we could use. It was for technical reasons that we were unable to. According to calculations established by statics experts, it seemed that the 8th floor was the very heart of the hospital, and that the pillars there were key to the building's stability. It seems that the intention behind the first shelling was to destroy those, and in that case, had they been successful, the four floors above us would have crumbled. Fortunately, that's not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Something I heard from Dr. Mandilovic, he said only one side of the hospital was hit, mostly the side facing the front; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The south side, that was not the confrontation line. It was an area held by the Serb forces. And the hospital overlooks that area. If you were watching CNN at the time, you would have seen a huge Red Cross flag hoisted on that side of the hospital. The front side had been virtually destroyed. This was deliberately targeted. They wanted to destroy that wing of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In that part of the front line, the confrontation lines were about 15 or 20 metres and went across both sides of the front line; right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, but back in 1992 nobody was even thinking that any of the Territorial Defence members might have a tank or might have targeted the hospital from a tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about that. I'm talking about the 10th of August 1994 and all the way to the very end of 1995. That's what I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you asked me about May just a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: May, yes.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which May?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: May 1992. All right. I did ask that but I know why I asked that. Now I am asking you, at the time during Dragomir Milosevic's time, was the hospital ever hit?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a far lesser degree. I did say that, didn't I.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was it ever targeted deliberately, the way Dr. Mandilovic described this? He said he wasn't sure.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the way it had been targeted in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't be looking for the reference now, but you say that one of your people -- that your staff often went to the front line to help the wounded and evacuate them, help evacuate them; right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the staff of the former military hospital and they went until as late as 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about this time. You went to the front line, your own medical staff went to the front line, what never?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about any other front line?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. What about you personally? Did you ever take that tunnel out of town? Did you ever leave town by that tunnel?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Whoever wanted to, as long as they had permission --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they could all leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the fact that throughout the whole autumn of 1994 there was an electricity cable going through the tunnel, electricity generated at Neretva, Mount Igman; the cable was going through this tunnel. This was all built at the time using a minimum of electricity. And between autumn 1994 and until the very end, Sarajevo had a very good electricity supply; right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Sarajevo was virtually smothered. It was the only possible ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There is something in your statement, 002 -- 65 ter 002842. On page 1 of the English, it's page 1, the first paragraphs, the first items or bullets, the first four or five, I suppose. I provided the reference. It's the 26th of September, 2001. Can you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I still have the old one. Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 02842.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that now, sir?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still have the same screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is supplemental information sheet provided by Dr. Bakir Nakas on the 26th of September, 2001. Page 1 of both the English and the B/C/S, 65 ter 02842.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this the document which is on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see what you say there. The first bullet: "Military casualties were taken by all the hospitals, but this one the most, as a number of former staff doctors were assigned to units in the field and gave front line treatment ..." So you say that your own medical staff did go to the front line.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who had been mobilised, the staff who had been mobilised, then they were members of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did they go back to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were out in the field the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever notice them being deliberately targeted? So this is a dangerous question for my own client. That's how far I'm going. Were any of those ever deliberately targeted?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the doctors?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the year, but it may have been the year when outside the war hospital at Igman, Dr. Dragan Stevanovic was hit. He lost his foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I was asking about members --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an employee of my hospital, regardless of his ethnicity. Serb or non-Serb, he was a hospital employee.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about how the nurses and the medical staff got killed at Igman? Autumn of 1994, a huge scandal erupted over this. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about bullet 2, where you say that SkyNews and other journalist groups stayed here and were located on the 12th floor. You spoke about that a wile ago. They filmed night shelling from there in 1992. Stayed a month or so then occasional visits. Then you go on to speak about a Van Lynden who you say was well known to you. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having taken over the hospital in May 1992, the responsibility of the hospital as a general manager, several groups of journalists were announced to me at the time, I mean their arrival. The most famous among those was the SkyNews crew. The application was about publishing images and footage from Sarajevo, and they wished to use the highest floors of our hospital for that purpose. We tried to dissuade them by telling them that this was risky business, indeed. And despite this, the SkyNews crew went up to the 12th floor of the hospital, and on several occasions they managed to take footage of the night shelling of Sarajevo. They would stay several weeks at a time. And normally they were in the northern sector of Sarajevo which was not directly next to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did they ever film any shells that were launched on the Serb side? Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to ask a question and I would like to hear what your position is on that. It concerns what the doctor described as stress that they had been exposed to, himself and the citizens of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that, but there were also 40.000 Serbs in Sarajevo suffering from the same stress.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the people who lived in Sarajevo were equally exposed to the level of stress, regardless of their ethnicity, whether they were Serbs, Croats, or Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to clarify one point please before Defence counsel moves on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We now have the French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before Defence counsel moves on to another subject, I would like to clarify one point. You discussed the doctors and nurses who were killed at Mount Igman; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That's what the counsel said. I mentioned one of my doctors who was mobilised for the BH army who was wounded on Mount Igman. The counsel was mentioning a completely different incident and I never confirmed remembering it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let's set aside what Defence counsel has said and let's concentrate on what you and your other colleagues mentioned about these people that were hit at Mount Igman. I would like to know in which year this occurred, because we have to stick to the indictment, of course. Were people hit during fighting operations? Was this person hit when he was a soldier or was he targeted because he was a doctor? Because he was wearing insignia which is usually -- or according to international conventions, he was wearing that kind of insignia. I didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said in my statement is that I cannot remember accurately whether it was in 1994. It is possible that it was in that year. The doctor was wounded right in front of the medical unit while he was treating the patients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning His Honour's question, let me just amend it somewhat. You know nothing about how numerous medical staff were massacred, members of the army of Republika Srpska, at Mount Igman, which was extensively described in General Rose's book and which became, thanks to his book, generally known fact. Did that happen during the tenure of General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could remember, I would have told you. I have no reason to withhold that. But at that time such information was not available in Sarajevo, nor can I remember anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand. I was asking you about the stress that everybody was exposed to. I would like to ask you about an additional stress that was laid on the Serbs, who, in Sarajevo in 1992, were being killed en masse. Do you know about the Serbs who disappeared or were killed in 1992, not in war operations?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born in Sarajevo and I have many friends among Serbs. A number of them, as well as a number of Bosniak and Croat left Sarajevo. It was their decision. Those who remained in Sarajevo, including myself, were never either maltreated or got killed. I'm talking about my friends with whom I spent those four years. The stories that there was maltreatment and persecution of Serbs by others were circulated, and some of the perpetrators were prosecuted in Sarajevo. I think that was in 1993 -- 1992 and 1993, and some convictions were even made. But I personally know no such person that was either killed or went missing among my friends. And that equally applies to the members of my staff. There were many Serbs on my staff and nothing ever happened to them. I was a victim of harassment in 1992 when I left JNA --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the killings and the persecutions.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were stories about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And there were people who were convicted of these crimes.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a widespread fear that anyone -- that this could happen to anyone?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was fear that this same thing could happen equally to the Bosnian Croats and everyone else. They could have been taken to the lines to dig trenches and be maltreated by units that did not follow the spirit of the rules of conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were they active inside Sarajevo as well?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This concludes my cross-examination. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Ms. Marcus?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, except that I would just like to tender the -- I know I tendered the two spreadsheets relating to the hospital records, but I don't believe that we tendered the underlying -- the actual hospital records which underlie those spreadsheets. So I'd just like to tender that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As these involve spreadsheets, we'll adopt the same procedure that we did. The court deputy will, overnight, assign the various numbers and tomorrow we'll admit it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Doctor, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for giving it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution calls Sanela Dedovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And while that's being done, I take the opportunity to give a decision on the Prosecution motion of the 9th of January, which requested protective measures for a number of witnesses, including W-138. The Defence has not responded to this motion. In court, on the 24th of January, the Prosecution noted that W-138 had previously been granted the requested protective measures in Galic. W-138 is scheduled to testify on Tuesday, 30th January, and consequently we now address the request for protective measures. We note that W-138 was previously granted pseudonym and voice and image distortion in Galic. This is evident from the transcript of the hearing on 14th April 2002 when the witness gave testimony with these protective measures. Under Rule 75(F)(i) of the Tribunal's Rules, protective measures that have been ordered in respect of a witness in any proceedings before the Tribunal continue to have effect mutatis mutandis in any subsequent proceedings unless and until they are rescinded, varied or augmented, in accordance with the procedure set out in that Rule. As a result, the Prosecution need only have requested a variation of the pseudonym. Therefore, the Trial Chamber confirms that the protective measures of pseudonym and voice and image distortion will extend to the present proceedings. The only variation on those protective measures is the pseudonym itself, and in that regard the Trial Chamber considers that the witness is to be referred to as W-138.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please begin by telling us all your name.

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Sanela Dedovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Ms. Dedovic, how old are you?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm 26. I'll be 26 in June this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And what city and country did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: In the city of Sarajevo, in the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you still live in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you live in Sarajevo throughout the siege of 1992 through 1995?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm going to be asking you some questions about something that happened to you during that siege, but before I do, did you meet with an investigator from this Tribunal on 13 November 1995?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And since coming to The Hague last week, have you had the opportunity to read that statement over carefully?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had the opportunity to read that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: In what language did you read it?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: In Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And when you read that statement over, can you confirm that that was a true and correct account of what you told the investigator on 13th of November, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everything is exactly as I said and what I said in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Later, on the 20th of April, 2006, did you again meet with an investigator, a different investigator this time, but still from this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, again, since arriving in The Hague last week, have you had an opportunity to read that statement over carefully?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: In what language did you read the statement of 20th April 2006?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: In Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And was everything in that statement true and correct when you re-read it last week or perhaps over the weekend?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Exactly as the statement I gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, pursuant to Rule 92 ter of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, I offer the statements of 13 November 1995 and 20 April 2006 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please give them a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement 13 November 1995 becomes P109, and the statement 20th of April, 2006, will become P110.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Ms. Dedovic, I just have a few questions concerning the events. Were you shot during the siege of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you remember the date on which you were shot?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: It was the 22nd November 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you mentioned a couple of minutes ago how old you are today. How old were you on the 22nd of November, 1994?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: I was 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Were you still in school?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was, elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The area where you were shot, did you think that that was a dangerous area?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And was there a safer way to go than the way you went, which I understand took you out into an open square where three roads come together? Was there a safer way to get where you were going?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was another route which we took between the houses and through gardens in order to get some -- at least some protection. But this was also exposed to sniper fire from Spicaste Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Were you wearing new shoes on the 22nd of November, 1994?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I put on my new tennis shoes and I decided to run across this junction, because the day before it was raining and it was muddy to go through this backyard and garden, so I decided to run across this junction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So you didn't want to get your new shoes dirty?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as a little girl, that's what I decided. And I wanted to walk to town in my new tennis shoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And new shoes can be important -- more important to a 12-year-old girl than to a woman of 25, I take it?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: On the 22nd of November, 1994, what was the weather like?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the weather that day was dry, but the day before it was raining.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Let me ask a little different question. What was the visibility like on the 22nd of November, 1994? Was there anything that would make it -- like fog, that would make it difficult for a person to see more than a few hundred metres?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That was slightly leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Slightly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no fog, which means that the visibility was good. It was all clear. You could see everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Were there -- when you were on your walk, did you see any Bosnian soldiers or other military equipment?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Was there any fighting, any armed combat, going on in the area?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was also a leading question, did she see the soldiers, et cetera. The witness I mean. I would have understood if it would have put him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty asked, did she see any soldiers, and perhaps you could then ask about the ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I can do it that way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Let's back up and do that again, Ms. Dedovic. On your walk that day, before you got shot, did you see any soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: There were no soldiers there, so I didn't see anyone. I was alone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you see any military equipment?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you see any combat, any fighting between soldiers, going on?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No. That was a quiet day, and that's why I decided to run across this junction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Ms. Dedovic, now I've got some questions about where this took place, and I'm going to ask you to take a look at a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please have displayed on the monitor a map with 65 ter number 2872.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're still waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand this takes quite some time to be processed and it's on its way. It's here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: It's here. And if I could then ask, could we please scroll to the north-east area of the city of Sarajevo, that would be the upper right-hand corner of this map. Thank you. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then lastly, Ms. Dedovic, do you see a map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- you said earlier that you grew up in Sarajevo. Did you grow up in a specific --

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: -- a specific neighbourhood or district of Sarajevo; and if so, could you tell us the name?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I grew up in Sarajevo, at Sedrenik, in the old city.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is the area of Sedrenik on the map that is on the monitor in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please zoom it a little bit more, if possible. It's right here. You need to go a little further up with the map. Right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And if I could ask the registrar to assist the witness in using the pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Just draw a circle on the map indicating Sedrenik.

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The second thing I'll ask you to mark on that map is, can you find the intersection where you were shot on the 22nd of November, 1994?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please zoom in a little more on this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Ms. Dedovic, I'm sorry, we can't zoom in, because if we do we'll lose the circle you've already drawn. Is it possible for you to -- if it's not possible, that's all right. We'll move on. This is not a test. But we can't zoom in on this map, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I -- perhaps this is the way to proceed: Could I please tender the map as marked now, and then we'll start over with a clean map, we'll expand the upper right-hand corner to the point where the witness is comfortable and have her mark that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we can proceed that way.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be admitted as Exhibit P111, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's now time for the break, in fact. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Ms. Dedovic, on the monitor in front of you now we have an unmarked copy of this map. I believe it's in evidence as Exhibit P104, and I'm going to ask the registrar to zoom in once or twice until -- is this close enough, or do you want it closer yet?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: It's close enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask the registrar to assist you in using the marking pen, and I'm going to ask you to draw a circle around the intersection where you were shot on 22nd of November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And would you mind writing a letter S beside that circle so we know what it is for.

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Right here. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'll ask, do you see a hill marked on that map called Sedam Suma?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, it's not actually written on the map, but does the hill Sedam Suma have, or is it near to another feature called Sharpstone?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: It's all connected, Sedam Suma and Spicaste Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could you use the pen and show us where Sharpstone is. Just draw a line for Sharpstone.

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Should I do it like this? [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I just want to make clear, is that line running along Sharpstone or is that some sort of an arrow pointing to Sharpstone? Because I notice that you've drawn it right into the circle marked S. That's why I ask the question.

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a line connecting Spicaste Stijena and it's as the crow flies from the traffic junction to Spicaste Stijena, or Sharpstone. But, you know, it's a bit like this. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. And then just for the record, could we indicate that the second line you drew, could you mark that SS? I won't try and say Spicaste Stijena in Bosnian but ... I'm sorry, I ...

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps here, this is where I should mark. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And now, Ms. Case Manager, if we could please have the panoramic shot of sniping -- scheduled sniping incident number 7. And if I could please tender the map that is currently on the monitor into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let it be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P112, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And we're done with the pen at this point, Mr. Registrar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Ms. Dedovic, now on the monitor in front of you there is an aerial photograph. Do you recognise what's in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the junction where I was hit or wounded, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: There's a red circle in the middle of a square. Do you see the red circle?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is that red circle on the place where you were shot? Is it in the right place?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And when you were in -- can you tell us where Sharpstone would be in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Spicaste Stijena is this way, as the crow flies. This photograph may, in fact, have been taken from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. So just to make sure I've understood you properly, the photographer may have been standing on Sharpstone when he or she took this picture.

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And now, Ms. Case Manager, could we please click on the red circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, Ms. Dedovic, we're going to do a 360-degree view from that circle, and I'm going to ask you at the end if this was a fair and accurate photograph of the area where you were shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Can we proceed, please. And could we rotate, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can stop right there. Right there, this is where I was. I was crossing the junction, and Spicaste Stijena is the hill that you can see over there. And this was the location of the sniper, right in the middle of the hill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is the junction? I don't see a junction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I don't either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We just passed it or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: We'll see it again. We'll rotate through a number of streets, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Ms. Dedovic, when you say "that hill," we can't really see where you're pointing because we can't see your monitor. So for purposes of clarity, there is a hill in the picture with a line of trees on the top of that. Is that the hill you're referring to, or is it a different hill?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that hill over there, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Right. And if we --

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: On the right-hand side of the photograph, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecutor has just done something that he is not supposed to do. They were leading the witness. They said, "Is this the hill or the forest from which there was sniping?" This is no way to go about examining a witness. The witness should be able to tell us herself. And now it is being put to the witness that shots were fired from this forest, and Spicaste Stijena, after all, is a broad concept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Point us to the part --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Prosecution leading to the witness, putting to the witness, where the shots came from; that this was Spicaste Stijena and that that was where the shots came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And this is an instance of something that is important to the Defence, where the shot came from, whether it came from a hill, and where the hill was. So, Mr. Docherty, there is merit in the submission that you led the witness as to a point of contention, and that is not permissible. The evidence then has very little value when you lead like that. You must let the witness give the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be heard on that point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only thing I was trying to do, and I apologise if I crossed the line, is that the witness was pointing at her monitor and saying things like, "here and here," and I was trying to clarify. And given that there is only one hill in the photograph, I understood I was leading, but given that there is only one hill, I thought the risk was low. But I do apologise. Ms. Case Manager, could we resume the rotation, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Ms. Dedovic, you've watched that photograph all the way through 360 degrees. Is that a fair and accurate picture of the location where you were shot?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's accurate. This is the junction in Sedrenik, Perugina, Racaga [phoen], Gorasanovic [phoen], that's the junction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender the -- this 360-degree view and the overhead photograph that preceded it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let it be numbered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P113, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Ms. Dedovic, do you have an opinion as to where it was that the bullet that hit you came from that day?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: My opinion is the bullet came from Spicaste Stijena. I was facing the other way. I was coming from over there. I was about to cross the junction in order to reach Rogina Street. From there I would not have had the Spicaste Stijena within my view because the slope was a downward one. Therefore, had I headed down that slope, I would no longer have had Spicaste Stijena within my view. It was from behind me that the bullet came. It couldn't possibly have come from anywhere else other than Spicaste Stijena, and we all knew that there was a sniper there, a sniper's nest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When you say "we all knew," who is "we"?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Civilians, mostly civilians, local residents of that neighbourhood. There was a sign there saying, "Caution: Sniper."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then lastly, as we look at this photograph, we're looking slightly down a hill. Do you see a road going down a hill a little bit?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I just want to get the direction that you were going. Were you going up or were you going down?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: I was coming from down there. I was walking up and then I came here, a little further up. That's as far as I got, the piece of even ground that you can see in the photograph. I had gone a little further on, and by this time I had reached the middle of the junction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, this is a matter that I've been thinking about for some time --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- with this technology available to us. The evidence that she has just given, pointing to where she was walking from and exactly where she was when she was shot, that may be a matter of importance, but we haven't been able to see that -- those marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: There are no marks, Your Honour, and my understanding is that we can't mark on these videos because they come up on the -- well, it's the monitor on your right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's the point I'm making, because under the old system, you would put the map on the ELMO and she would have marked it, and then we would have had the benefit of seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So we have a description from her in words, but we haven't actually been able to see the mark, and so the evidence doesn't have the impact on us that it should. And I feel somewhat disadvantaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm making use of the technology that I was -- that's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In my view, the older system with the ELMO where you can mark the map, and then we can see, was more advantageous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I believe that for important photographs like this one, maybe it would be nice to also have a hard copy that we could put on the ELMO so that the witness can actually mark it, because right now we have no idea what really happened. It's really difficult to reconstruct the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you wanted to say something on this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely. I'm not sure if it's my turn to cross-examine. I wanted to change tack if it's my turn, if that photograph could please be kept, for this photograph to be kept for the beginning of my cross-examination, as soon as it is my turn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, well, that will be noted. Yes. Mr. Docherty, this, of course, is not a criticism of you. It's just a comment on the system, and I hope it is taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, anything the Chamber says, Your Honour, is taken into account, and we will -- well, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do I understand, then, that whenever markings are done on a map on the e-court system, as she was just marking that map, we can't see the markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That is not my understanding, Your Honour. My understanding is as follows, and I am not a technology expert, but my understanding is that we put in the clean map, and that's in as P104. The witness then marks on that map and then the marked copy goes into evidence as, I think in this case, P110. Then the witness marks on it again and that again goes into evidence, and any one of these can be called up and looked at by the parties or by the Chamber, if they know how to do it or can have someone help them bring it up. They can be brought up at any time. And that's why when a witness finishes marking on a map, I always say, May I tender the marked-up copy of the map? And that way we have both the clean map and the marked-up map in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So in principle, the markings on that map could be brought up on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That is correct. Any marked map can be brought up on your screen. And we've used this same map over and over again. And all of those different markings have been preserved. This witness has marked on it twice. You'll recall she had difficulty until we zoomed in. So we have a clean map, we've got a map where she's circled Sedrenik, and we've got a map where she's indicated the intersection and Sharpstone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the markings that she just made as to where she was walking from and where she was, can that be brought up now?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: No, because she didn't make markings. We can mark on the map but we can't mark on photographs and things like that. Rather, we can mark on some exhibits but not others, and I'm sorry, I don't know all the technical ins and outs. But the witness made no markings on this, and I knew she would not be able to, which is why I put the question, Were you going uphill or downhill, because that's really the only way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And I thought you said, "this is where I was," so that's why I had the impression she was pointing to a particular place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The witness was saying, I was here and I was there, but she was simply pointing with her finger and no marks were resulting. That's why I had to clarify the record by saying uphill or downhill because I understood that no markings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's my point. For that evidence to be most helpful to us, we should be able to see those points.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I agree with that. We do have a video that we're about to show that may help, where the witness points out where she was and where she was coming and where she was going, and that will be my next exhibit and also the end of my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And now, Ms. Case Manager, there was a video with this witness, and I'd ask to have that played for the Court at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: "Investigator: Witness, at this time I'd like you to please stand in the location and in the position you were on the 22nd of November, 1994, when you were wounded. "Can you please point in the direction that you were moving. "Okay. That's fine. If you could come back, please. "And if you could please point to the location on your body where you were wounded. "Thank you. Can you please point in the direction from which you believe the shot came from on that day. "Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Ms. Dedovic, do you remember that encounter with the investigator and making this video?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And was the video we just saw an accurate video? Is that actually what happened with the investigator on the day the video was made?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's accurate. It's just the way it was. It shows the direction in which I was moving, the way I was facing, and that Spicaste Stijena was behind me, that I was walking away from it. And I had got as far as the midpoint of that junction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, I'm sorry to get back to this, is this the way that you'd be dealing with this kind of situation, by presenting a video after the witness has looked at the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, it was the way that I was planning to do it from now on. However, if the Chamber is not finding that persuasive, believe me, I'll change it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm just dealing with it, getting back to the technical point --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- because that somehow I think compensates, although not fully, for the fact that we're not able to see the markings that she made. I just want to have confirmed that when she made those markings on the map, because it was a map --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The markings were made on the map, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- it doesn't -- the fact that we were not able to see it is not a reflection on our technical competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's the technology.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That's the technology, but those markings have not disappeared. That exhibit can be called back up and examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, I have one question to make things really clear. You showed us which way the bullet came from, according to you, but I'm not sure I really understood. You did not say where you were hit on your body. I don't know if you were very clear when it comes to that. Could you please tell us exactly where you were hit on your body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bullet, the shot that came, first ricocheted against the ground, against the asphalt, it splintered, and then a bit of shrapnel hit my ankle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a fragmentation bullet, which means that if I'd been hit directly in the leg, the injury would have been more severe. This way, when I underwent surgery, they first had to extract this piece of shrapnel from my leg or my ankle bone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Judge Mindua, I believe, has just asked the most relevant question. I can perhaps drop most of my questions and thereby cut short my cross-examination. Can we please have back on our screens the photograph that we had. Not the rotating one, the one that has no persons in it. That's the one I'd like to have. Thank you. Yes, that's right. That's the right one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please point -- use her hand to show where the small circle is, roughly speaking. Madam Witness, where the small circle is, is that where you were standing? If you can see the photograph.

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The small circle.

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: It was further up. It was further up that I was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's try to draw a line between your position as you showed that investigator, sort of a little to the right, in that general direction. You pointed out the location of Spicaste Stijena. What about your position? Can you answer this one, please: Between your position and the position where you say the sniper was, do you know that between the two there were BH army positions? Do you know that as a fact? Otherwise, the army of Republika Srpska could have crossed the area any time they liked. However, the truth of the matter is there were BH army positions between your position and the position that the shot had come from.

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Serb army were at Spicaste Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about your men?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: They were further down at the foot of Spicaste Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So the confrontation line ran along the entire length of Spicaste Stijena; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Sanela, I have no intention of cross-examining you for a long time. I merely wish to bring up some things that you mentioned in your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you asked her, "Between your position and the position where you say the sniper was, do you know that between the two there were BH army positions?" What's the answer to that? I'm asking you, Miss, the counsel asked you to confirm that there were BH army positions between the position where you say the sniper was and the position where you were. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the defence forces were at the foot of Spicaste Stijena. The Serb soldiers were up there on top of Spicaste Stijena and the BH army were at its foot. That's where the defence line was. Had it not been for the defence forces there, one could not have gone on leading normal lives, or indeed, staying there at all. There had to be some defence there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your answer to the question, then, is yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The defence forces were at the foot of Spicaste Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be skipping all these questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just have one more question. What was the distance between the place where the BH army forces were and where you were? What was the approximate distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The distance would be about 3 kilometres or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the distance between the position where the Serb army was and where you were, what's the approximate distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be the same, the same distance. They were at or around Spicaste Stijena and the defence forces were at the foot of it. They were up there and the Bosnian defence line was further down, at the foot of the hill. The distance should be roughly the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Roughly the same, yes. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thanks to what we've just heard, I am now able to skip most of my questions, save for a few. The first thing I wanted to start with was the later statement. Can we please have DD00-0356 brought up on our screens, please. This one bears the following date: The 13th of November, 1995, which is soon after the end of fighting in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have that in front of you? Page 1, please. In actual fact, there is only one page. Yes, I said it right. DD00-0356. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: All I have is the map. Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Page 2. There, that's the statement. Do you have the B/C/S version in front of you, the Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Here it is. Can you take a look at the middle of the page, the sentence begins with, "I would say ..." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "I would say that the confrontation line is about 200 to 300 metres of air line from the position where you were." Is that correct? And from the place where you were standing and the place where the confrontation line was, was the distance 2 to 300 metres, as you said in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Around 300 metres?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And then further on you said that a piece of metal had been extracted from your leg in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you said, "I assume that the bullet first hit the ground behind me, a bit on the left side, and that it split in fragments. One fragment entered above my ankle, behind my left leg, a little bit on the left side." Correct?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: May I say that you did not receive a direct hit, but that rather the bullet first fragmented and then hit you.

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The bullet first fragmented against the asphalt surface, because at that moment I started running.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Why did you start running? Did you hear shots?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear shots. I started running because of safety. I wanted to cross this junction as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear one shot fired before that?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear anything. Everything was quiet. I started crossing the intersection, and for my own safety, I decided to speed up a little bit and run. And at that moment I first felt pain and then I heard the sound of the shot. Then I saw blood and I was hopping on one foot. And when UNPROFOR came, they were the only ones who were able to approach me, because another shot came afterwards preventing anyone else from approaching the intersection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like you to see another document that I received from the Prosecution. It's been translated into English. It's DD00-0363. It's a statement of yours that you gave on the premises of the police on the 10th of March, 1995. Do you remember giving this statement?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the Serbian version -- I mean the Bosnian version?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to compare this with anything else, but this is a statement that you gave to Omer Isanovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says, that I gave this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, I have another document, DD00-0362, another document that I received from the Prosecution of which I couldn't find a translation, compiled on the 22nd of November, 1994, which means on the day when you were shot. This official note, compiled by Kemal Ibisevic, has it been presented to you on that particular day? And more importantly, were you made aware of the following, that says in this document? Can you see this official note?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 3: "Upon receipt of information, the investigating judge on duty of the High Court in Sarajevo, Nermina Mutalvolic [phoen] was notified, but she did not visit the scene because an on-site investigation could not have been conducted due to incessant sniping against the area." Did you make that statement?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You don't remember; is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said that I cannot remember that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Because if that was the case, it means that up there at Sedrenik there was shooting along the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no shooting in terms of attacks or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you see, the investigating judge did not dare go to the scene because of the shooting.

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what happened later, whether there was any shooting or not when I was already at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have one more question relating to your statement given on the 20th of April, 2006. It's DD00-0344. I originally intended to dwell more on this one; however, I only have one question. Can you please look at the last page. That's actually page 2. And I think it's also page 2 in the English version. Page 2 of the statement. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the last passage, which reads: "During the war, there were some periods where there seemed to be no shelling or shooting," et cetera. "Sometimes there would be many days or even weeks where there would be no sniping from Sharpstone, and we would say that there was somebody nice in that sniper position." Was that in the last year of war?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we children used to say, that there must be a nice man up there who wouldn't fire from the sniper rifle, and that's why it seemed that the day was quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was that in the last year of war?

utterances.speaker: SANELA DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender document DD00-0362 into evidence, and as well -- and also the document DD00-0363, if possible, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I believe those are in evidence, Your Honour. I believe these are the statements that we 92 terred at the beginning of the witness' examination-in-chief. And the statement to the Bosnian police officer would have been incorporated within the first statement, because the witness says, "I have had read to me a statement I gave to the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I confirm that it is my own." That is the opening of the 1995 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. We'll ask the court deputy if he can confirm that they are already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't able to locate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The court deputy says his records don't show that either of these documents has already been admitted. But I tell you what we'll do, in view of the ambiguity, please proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic, and I'll ask the court deputy to further investigate the matter. We'll come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you, but I have no further questions. I have wrapped up my cross-examination. As far as I know, these documents have not been entered into evidence under 65 ter and therefore I insist on them being entered as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They will be entered one way or the other. It's just that I've been alerted to what Mr. Docherty said, which is that they are statements of the witnesses and normally these are tendered during examination-in-chief. So it's just a matter of having it confirmed if they have already been entered. If they haven't been, they will be tendered as exhibits by the Defence, and I'll ask the court deputy to check on that. Now, is there any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: No, there is not, Your Honour. And just so the record is clear, I was not opposing the admission of these documents. I just thought they might be getting duplicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The court deputy will get back to me on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
